name: Brísingamen
powers: Heightens the beauty of its wearer; a treasure of the goddess Freyja.
description: Brísingamen, the necklace of the goddess Freyja, is one of the great treasures of the Norse gods, forged by the dwarves. The Prose Edda lists it among the wealth of the gods, and in the poem Lokasenna Loki taunts Freyja that she had to sleep with each of the four dwarves who made it to obtain it — a story expanded in the later Sörla þáttr, where Freyja is described as bartering her favours for the jewel. The necklace is also central to the legend of the hero Þórólfr and to the tale of the god Heimdallr and Loki, who fought over it in the shape of seals at Singasteinn; Heimdallr recovered it for Freyja. The name is sometimes taken to mean 'bright' or 'gleaming' necklace, and the jewel later became a model for Freyja's shining golden hair of amber. Brísingamen remains a standard example of the dwarven treasure hoard in retellings of Norse myth.

name: Bjargástafur
powers: Carries the bearer through danger and hardship unharmed.
description: Bjargástafur, the 'rescue stave' or 'saving stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that the bearer could escape or survive any danger. Its name derives from the verb bjarga, 'to save', and the grimoire tradition promises that no misfortune could hold a person who bore it, whether on land, at sea, or in a dispute. It is one of the general talismans of protection in Icelandic folk magic, carried on paper, carved on wood, or worn on the person in times of peril. Like all the galdrastafir, its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that gathered older material, and it is now widely reproduced in books and on jewellery. The rescue stave remains popular today as a general symbol of safety and deliverance.

name: Bridal Crown
powers: Marks the bride as a crowned bride, bringing honour to the wedding.
description: The bridal crown (brudkrona), a crown of gilt silver or brass that Swedish churches owned and lent to brides for the wedding ceremony. The custom, recorded from the Middle Ages, made the bride a 'crowned bride' and the crown a symbol of honour and virginity. Rules sometimes required a fee, and the crown was kept locked in the church between weddings. The crown became common in Sweden only after the Reformation, when it spread from the nobility and the towns to country parishes in the seventeenth century; it was usually owned by the parish itself, lent out for the wedding and locked away again afterwards. Made of gilt silver with red and green glass set in imitation of gems, it recalled the crown of the Virgin Mary, and a bride who had once worn it was said to keep that honour for life. The fee charged for the lending supported the church, and the rules could be strict: the crown was returned the same day, and its use bound the bride to a good name.
source: Swedish church custom of the bridal crown

name: The Barrel Bung
powers: Conjures food, drink, or gold for its owner.
description: A barrel bung, the wooden stopper of a cask, that works magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Barrel Bung', the small wooden plug proves able to conjure food, drink, or gold for its owner. It is one of the many humble objects that Swedish wonder-tales turn into providers of plenty. In the Swedish telling, famine has dried the parish of Bolinge while the rich Lady Skinflint's cows never fail; the boy Jerker discovers why — she keeps an enchanted barrel that gushes milk whenever the bung is drawn. When she hides the bung, the barrel is only wood and iron, and the king's men find nothing; Jerker must watch and wait until the bung is carried back, then seize it in a single dash. The magic bung, once stolen, feeds the whole starving village through the winter, and the boy is rewarded with wool and silver for his courage. The tale makes the smallest of farm objects the key to plenty and to justice.

name: The Bewitched Knife
powers: Steel laid across the cradle keeps the changeling away; a knife breaks spells.
description: An iron knife that Swedish folk tradition used against harmful magic, one of the many protective uses of steel and iron in Nordic belief. A knife or other steel object laid across a newborn's cradle was believed to keep the bortbyting, the changeling, from swapping the child, and similar iron was set under the birthing bed and over the stable door to hold off trolls and the mare. A knife was also run through a bewitched churn, struck into the threshold, or thrown over the roof to break a spell that had soured the milk or the luck of a farm. The sign-carved knife served the healer in 'signing' rites, where a knowledgeable woman or man traced protective marks and spoke a formula over the sick. Iron's power to turn the hidden folk and their magic is one of the oldest and most widespread motifs of Scandinavian folk belief, surviving into the 20th century in rural custom.
source: Swedish folk belief in steel against harmful magic

name: The Broom King
maker: The broom itself in the tale
powers: Rules all brooms and sweeps away the story's dangers.
description: The broom king, the broom that rules all brooms, from the Swedish tale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'. In the tale a broom proves to be the king of its kind, sweeping away the story's dangers with a command that no other broom could match. The tale plays on the humble household object raised to kingship, a comic inversion in the spirit of the Scandinavian wonder-tales where the lowliest tool of the house shows the greatest power. The broom was in any case no ordinary thing in folk belief, being used to sweep out evil at the threshold, to sweep luck into the house at New Year, and as a mount in the lore of witches. Making the broom a king gathers all that magic into one homely hero, and the tale delights in seeing the farmyard champion reign.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'

name: The Black Book of the Clergy
powers: Conjurations and signs for summoning and binding spirits.
description: The black book (svartbok), a manual of black magic that Swedish tradition placed in the hands of a priest or 'klok' man who had studied 'the black art'. Actual svartkonstböcker, filled with conjurations, signs, and instructions, survive in Swedish archives from the 17th-19th centuries, and they mix prayers, biblical names, and runic-looking signs in the same hand that kept the parish register. Legend said the priest's black book could be passed on only on his deathbed, since the book had been given him by the powers of the dark and would burn or vanish if it fell to an unworthy hand. The book was used to find thieves, heal the bewitched, conjure answers, and bind spirits, and it made the clergy who owned it feared as much as respected. The black book stands at the meeting-point of church and folk magic, where the man of God was also the master of the dark art.

name: Bukkehorn
description: A natural folk horn cut from a hollowed goat or cow horn and sounded through a mouthpiece pierced in the side. Herders used it on the summer seter pastures and at festive gatherings, carrying loud calls and dance tunes across mountain valleys. The horns range from small finger-hole instruments to long curved signal horns, and survived into the 20th century in Norwegian oral folk music. The bukkehorn's voice was part of the pastoral soundscape of the high pastures, heard alongside the kulokk and the shepherd's whistle, and each herder had his own way of making it carry. In the 20th century the instrument was revived in folk-music ensembles and is played again on the seter and in concerts, keeping the old mountain calls alive.

name: Bunad
material: Wool and linen with silver brooches
description: The festive national costume of Norway, sewn from wool in patterns that vary by district, with embroidery, silver brooches, and distinct headwear. Modern bunads grew out of the folk dress of the 18th and 19th centuries and were revived and standardized in the 20th as a symbol of national identity. Hundreds of regional variants are worn at holidays, weddings, and Constitution Day. Each bunad is made to a pattern from a particular valley or town, with the cut of the skirt, the colour of the cloth, and the shape of the headdress marking the wearer's district, and the silver brooches and buckles, often inherited, carry the family's history. The revival was led by folk-costume societies and the Husflid movement, which researched old garments and codified the modern forms. The bunad is worn with pride across Norway and is a living record of regional dress made national.

name: Borgund Stave Church
description: The best-preserved of Norway's stave churches, built around 1180 at Borgund in Sogn and never drastically altered since. Its stacked tiers of steep gabled roofs, four carved dragon-head finials, and decorated west portal are the classic image of the stave church, and the interior keeps medieval furnishings, runic graffiti cut by medieval visitors, and one of the oldest surviving altars in Norway. The building stands today much as its builders left it, its timber frame and tarred shingles intact, and it has served as the model for church designs and for the stave-church revival of the 19th century. It is owned by the Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments.

name: Bridle of Bellerophon
maker: Brought by Athena in a dream
powers: Tamed the winged horse Pegasus so Bellerophon could ride it against the Chimera.
description: The golden bridle Athena gave the Corinthian hero Bellerophon to tame the winged horse Pegasus, the instrument that let him ride the stallion and, mounted, destroy the fire-breathing Chimera of Lycia. Apollodorus records the dream in which Athena brought the bridle to Bellerophon as he slept at her altar, and the hero woke with the gift in his hand; later tellings place the meeting at the spring of Peirene on Corinth's acropolis. The bridle is an emblem of god-given mastery over a divine beast, and Pegasus, once bridled, served the hero through the trials laid on him by King Iobates, including the slaying of the Chimera. Pausanias reports that the bridle was preserved and dedicated in a temple of Athena Chalinitis, 'the Bridler', at Corinth, a relic claiming to be the very object of the legend. Its story shows how a seemingly small tool, a horse's bit, becomes the pivot of a hero's fate.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Pausanias, Description of Greece

name: Cauldron of Rebirth
powers: Restored slain warriors to life, though the revived could not speak.
description: Pair Dadeni, the Cauldron of Rebirth, appears in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, the story of Branwen daughter of Llŷr, where it is given to Bran the Blessed by a giant couple, Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife, who have carried it out of Ireland. Warriors slain in battle and cast into the cauldron are restored to life, though the revived come back unable to speak. When Bran invades Ireland to avenge the insult to Branwen, the cauldron is used to raise the enemy dead again and again, until Efnysien, the family's half-brother, destroys it by throwing himself into it and bursting it apart. The cauldron thus carries both the power of rebirth and the need for its own sacrifice. Scholars connect it with the Irish cauldrons of plenty and with the later Grail legends. Its story remains among the strangest and most discussed episodes of the Mabinogion.

name: Briar Rose's Spinning Wheel
powers: Pricked the princess and cast the whole castle into a hundred-year sleep.
description: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Briar Rose' (Dornröschen, KHM 50) is the instrument of the sleeping curse: the princess pricks her finger on its spindle, and the whole castle falls asleep for a hundred years. The king had ordered every spindle in the land burned to cheat the witch's prophecy, but an old woman in a forgotten tower still spins, and curiosity leads the princess to the fatal prick. When the prince at last cuts through the hedge of thorns and wakes the princess with a kiss, the spindle's curse is undone and the castle stirs back to life. The tale is the German form of the widespread Sleeping Beauty story, and the spinning wheel is its local signature, replacing the flax and distaff of older versions. Spinning in folklore is linked with fate, age and magic, so the wheel carries symbolic weight beyond the plot. The story was popularised in the Grimms' collection and in Perrault's and later cinematic retellings.

name: The Belt of Tahmineh
powers: Binds the bond between the lady of Samangan and the hero Rostam.
description: A belt said in some tellings of the story to have been woven by Tahmineh of Samangan, mother of Sohrab, and given to the hero Rostam on the night of their meeting, binding their union. The motif varies sharply across recensions of the Shahnameh and in modern retellings, and Ferdowsi's own text describes no single canonical belt, so the object's particulars rest on later tradition rather than on the epic's lines. In some versions Tahmineh also binds a token, a jewel or an armlet, on Sohrab so that the boy might one day know his father, and it is this token that drives the tragedy when father and son meet unknowing on the battlefield. The belt is therefore best read as a romantic elaboration of the episode, invented to give the doomed pair a visible bond, and any account of it must be marked as uncertain.

name: The Brazen Serpent
powers: Healed the Israelites bitten by desert serpents when they looked upon it.
description: The bronze serpent made by Moses at God's command to heal the Israelites bitten by serpents in the wilderness, raised on a pole so that the stricken who looked upon it lived, as told in the Book of Numbers. Kept for centuries in the Jerusalem Temple, it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah as an idol under the name Nehushtan, when the people had come to burn incense to it. Its story is told in Numbers and in 2 Kings, and the object itself is known only from scripture, with no archaeological trace. In later tradition the brazen serpent became a type of healing lifted up for all to see, and Christian exegesis read it as a foreshadowing of the cross, a reading that has kept the image alive in religious art for two thousand years.

name: Bagua Mirror
powers: Deflects harmful energy (sha qi) and returns evil glances
description: The bagua mirror is a circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy, sha qi, and to return an attacker's evil gaze. In domestic use it is placed above the main door or facing a threatening structure such as a road, a corner, or a neighbour's roof-ridge, so that the mirror deflects or reflects the influence back to its source. The mirror also appears in Daoist talismanic practice, paired with written spells against hauntings and possession, and the convex form is said to disperse harm while the concave form gathers or focuses it. Because of its power to reflect, the bagua mirror is one of the few feng shui remedies that practitioners advise using with care, lest the mirrored effect fall on an innocent. The object joins the practical science of geomancy to the older Chinese belief in mirrors as revealers of spirits, a connection that goes back to the bronze mirrors of the Han period.

name: Bangmangi
powers: Grants whatever the wielder wishes when struck
description: The bangmangi is the magic club of the dokkaebi, the mischievous goblin of Korean folklore, which grants whatever a person wishes when it is struck. In the folktales the dokkaebi owns the club and uses it to summon food, gold, and servants, and clever humans trick the gullible goblin into surrendering it: a thief or a poor man persuades the dokkaebi that a beating with the club will bring a blessing, then runs off with the prize. In other variants the club is swapped, or its possessor uses it to draw endless rice and healing, and the object is so tied to its owner that the dokkaebi and its bangmangi are nearly interchangeable in stories. The club appears in the collected Korean tales of Im Bang and Yi Ryuk and in the oral tradition of the pansori storytellers, and it remains a beloved fixture of Korean children's literature and animation. The bangmangi embodies the dokkaebi's double nature as both threat and source of luck.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
powers: Foundation of hospitality and marriage ritual
description: The betel and areca tray is the lacquered brass container that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the essential offering of Vietnamese hospitality, courtship, and marriage ritual. In the founding legend two twin brothers, Cao and Lang, loved the same woman; when the woman married Cao, Lang wandered away and died by a stream, and Cao, grieving, drowned himself; the woman then died too. The gods transformed the brothers into the areca tree and the betel vine that climbs it, and the woman into the limestone that binds their flavour, so that the chewing of betel and areca joins the three together in eternal kinship. The tray is presented at weddings as a symbol of this bond, offered to guests as a mark of respect, and placed before ancestors during rites. In village custom the exchange of betel seals a promise, and the phrase 'to invite betel' still means to ask for a daughter's hand. The tray is among the most symbolic household objects of Vietnamese culture.
source: Betel and areca legend; folk custom

name: The Bayon Smile
powers: The king's watchful presence over the kingdom
description: The Bayon smile is the serene, downcast smile of the great stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, built in the twelfth century under the Buddhist king Jayavarman VII. Scores of colossal faces, each several metres high, gaze from the four sides of the towers, and scholars debate whether they portray the king himself, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, or the fusion of the two in the king's consecrated image. Khmer legend and local tradition read the many faces as the king's presence watching over his kingdom from every direction, a gaze both compassionate and sovereign. The temple was the state temple of Jayavarman's capital, and its face-towers combine Mahayana Buddhist devotion with the Khmer tradition of the devaraja, the god-king. The Bayon smile has become the emblem of Angkor and of Cambodian identity, appearing on the national flag and in art worldwide as an image of serene royal power.

name: Birchbark Canoe
material: Birchbark over cedar frame with spruce root lashing
powers: Glides silently over lakes and rivers, light enough to carry.
description: The birchbark canoe, wiigwaasi-jiimaan in Ojibwe, is the light, silent and remarkably strong craft built of sheets of birchbark sewn over a cedar frame with spruce root and sealed with spruce gum, the great carrier of the Anishinaabe and other northern peoples. Light enough for one person to carry across a portage, a full canoe could still move families, furs and goods across hundreds of miles of lakes and rivers, which is why French traders and the voyageurs adopted it wholesale. Master builders selected a smooth-barked birch, stripped the bark in the right season, and shaped the craft with the same materials and joinery used for centuries. The canoe also runs through the region's stories, from the flying canoe of the Passamaquoddy to the journeys of culture heroes. Today a handful of carvers still build bark canoes, and museums preserve the finest examples of this northern engineering triumph.
source: Anishinaabe oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Bolas
material: Balls of stone or iron joined by braided hide cords
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Entangles the legs of running cattle or game.
description: The bolas, or boleadoras, are throwing weights of the South American plains: two or three stone or iron balls, often covered in hide, joined by braided cords of leather. The hunter or gaucho swings them overhead and releases them to wrap around the legs of fleeing cattle, horses or rheas, tangling the animal in an instant fall. The weapon was developed by the Indigenous peoples of the Pampas and Patagonia and adopted wholesale by the colonial herders, and chroniclers recorded its use among the Mapuche and Tehuelche; a heavier solid type, the bolas perdidas, was hurled at enemies in war. The gaucho made the bolas his own, and the tool became so identified with him that it appears throughout the gauchesque literature, most famously in José Hernández's epic poem Martín Fierro. Today it survives in the cattle country of Argentina and Uruguay, used by the last horse-riding vaqueanos and kept alive as a symbol of the pampas.

name: Batá Drum
material: Carved hardwood with animal hide heads
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Talks the language of the orishas at ceremony.
description: The batá is the consecrated drum of Cuban Santería, an hourglass-shaped instrument with two heads of different sizes, played in a set of three, the small okónkolo, the middle itótele and the great iyá, the mother drum that speaks the lead voices. The drums descend from the Yoruba bata of West Africa, carried to Cuba by enslaved people and kept alive behind the Catholic saints, and their rhythms are said to speak the language of the orishas during ceremonies, each rhythm belonging to a particular spirit. A consecrated batá has the orisha Añá installed within it, and only initiated male drummers, omo Añá, may play it; the drums are never allowed to touch the ground and are fed and dressed when not in use. Changó, the thunder deity, is held to be the drums' spiritual owner. The iyá leads and the smaller drums answer, and together they call the orishas down into the gathering; beyond the temple, batá rhythms entered Cuban music and from there the world, but the sacred instrument remains the heart of the religion it serves.
source: Cuban Santería practice and music studies

name: Benin Bronze Plaque
maker: Igbesanmwan guild casters of the Igun quarter
description: The Benin bronzes are the cast-brass plaques that once covered the pillars of the Oba's palace in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, depicting the king, his warriors, chiefs and courtiers in high relief against openwork backgrounds. They were made by the guild of the Igun quarter using lost-wax casting, a craft reserved for the palace, and they record royal history, court protocol, the regalia of office and even the Portuguese visitors who came to the coast in the sixteenth century. In 1897 a British punitive expedition took the city, looted the palace and carried thousands of objects to Europe, where they entered museums from London to Berlin; the word bronze is traditional, but most of the plaques are brass, an alloy of copper and zinc. The plaques have since become the center of one of the world's great restitution debates, as Nigeria and the museums negotiate their return. They remain masterpieces of African cast metalwork and a record of a kingdom that Europeans both traded with and destroyed.
source: British Museum collections; Edo court history and restitution scholarship

name: Bogolanfini Mud Cloth
description: Bogolanfini, the mud cloth of the Bamana of Mali, is a cotton textile painted by women with a dye of fermented river mud, worked over a yellow ground to leave dark geometric patterns that record proverbs, clan histories and the teachings of initiation. The cloth is made in a slow sequence: the cotton is washed and dyed with a yellow infusion of leaves, then the designs are drawn in mud, which reacts with the yellow to leave a deep brown-black as the background is rinsed away. The cloths were worn at initiations, by hunters, and by women at the turning points of life, and the patterns are held to protect the wearer and to carry the memory of the family. Since the 1980s bogolan has left the village for the fashion world, worn by Malian musicians and designers and celebrated as a national art. Each bolt of bogolanfini is a document of the society that made it, written in earth.

name: Baule Goli Mask
description: The goli is a round-faced, painted mask of the Baule people of the Ivory Coast, worn with a full costume during village celebrations, funerals, and the dances of the goli society. The word names a whole sequence of masks that appear in a fixed order, from the round kpan faces through animal forms to the large, frightening figured masks, a progression that retraces the Baule cosmos and the order of communal life. Male and female variants dance in pairs, and the female face, with its calm forehead and scarified temples, is regarded as the model of Baule beauty. The dance is closely tied to the goli spirit powers believed to enter the masked dancers, and the performances draw the entire village together at moments of joy and mourning. In Baule belief the mask is not decoration but a doorway for those powers, which is why its storage and handling follow strict tradition.

name: Bamum Beaded Throne (Mandu Yenu)
description: The Mandu Yenu is the royal throne of the Bamum kingdom of the Cameroon Grassfields, a carved wooden stool and footstool completely encased in glass beads, cowrie shells, and brass studs. Mandu Yenu means 'rich in beads', and the most famous example, made for the Bamum court in the nineteenth century, was given by King Njoya to the German Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1908 and now rests in Berlin; a near-identical copy he commissioned remains in the palace at Foumban. The carving carries royal symbols such as the two-headed snake and the spider of wisdom, while two large figures, the protective twins Mandu and Yenu, stand behind the seat, and smaller rifle-bearing figures on the footrest speak of military might. The beads from Europe and cowries from the Indian Ocean were costly imports, so the encrusted surface itself proclaimed the king's reach. In Bamum belief the throne was bound to the authority of the fon, and the Berlin throne remains central to debates over colonial-era restitution.
source: British Museum collections (Mandu Yenu of King Nsangu)

name: Bamileke Elephant Mask
era: Traditional, still used in chiefdom rites
description: Beaded elephant masks of the Cameroon Grassfields are worn by men's societies of the Bamileke and related peoples, who dance them at the funerals of notables, the installation of chiefs, and the festivals of the kwifo, the regulatory society that enforces chiefly authority. The mask takes the shape of an elephant head, with broad flat ears and a central trunk, and is built over carved wood or a cloth and raffia frame before being covered in glass beads in the royal colours of the chiefdom. The elephant, like the leopard, belongs to the forest powers that underwrite Grassfields kingship, and the mask links the wearer, the fon, and the world of the bush spirits. Only society members and people of rank may wear or even touch such masks, which are kept hidden and given offerings in the chiefdom's storehouses. Collections in European and American museums have carried the form worldwide, and Grassfields bead artists continue the tradition today.
source: Museum collections of Cameroon Grassfields royal arts

name: Buganda Royal Drum (Mujaguzo)
description: The mujaguzo are the royal drums of the Buganda kingdom of Uganda, a set of tuned drums kept in a sacred drum house and regarded as the spiritual king of the kingdom. Ganda tradition holds that Buganda has two rulers, the human kabaka and the drums, which never die, and the drums are sounded to announce the birth of a prince, the death of a kabaka, the call to war, and the great ceremonies of state. The principal drum, Kawulugumu, is the 'king among drums', and at a coronation the new kabaka must first visit the drum house, tighten its hide, and strike it to take up his rule; its companion Namanyonyi is spoken of as its wife. The drums are kept suspended above the ground and are smeared with ghee and beer in ritual care, guarded by custodians of the Butiko clan. When the kingdom was abolished in 1966 the drums were hidden away and survived, and they were brought out again for the coronation of 1993. The royal drum tradition remains a living institution of the kabaka's court.

name: Burnous Cloak
description: The burnous is the hooded, floor-length cloak of the Maghreb, worn by Amazigh (Berber) and Arab men across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. It is woven in one seamless piece from pure sheep's wool, often left in the natural cream or brown colour of the fleece or dyed, and it is fitted with a single pointed hood that can be drawn over the head in sun, wind or rain. In pre-modern times the burnous served as overcoat, blanket and sleeping bag for travellers and shepherds on the steppe, while a white burnous became the ceremonial dress of chiefs, religious leaders and notables, handed down as an honour and worn at weddings, feasts and festivals. The garment is also remembered in legend, since tribal saints and warriors are described in oral tradition as being wrapped in or given a burnous as a mark of protection and blessing. Today the burnous is worn mainly on formal occasions, but it remains a defining element of Maghrebi identity and appears in the national dress of several North African countries.

name: Brass Urli
description: The urli is the wide, shallow brass vessel of South India, most often associated with the kitchens and courtyards of Kerala and Tamil Nadu, where it holds water, flowers and floating candles for decoration or worship. Traditional urulis are hammered or spun from brass and bell metal with a flared rim, and in a Malayali home one may stand on the floor of the entrance hall piled with fresh flowers, or be pressed into service as a cooking and storing pot for rice and water. In temples and festivals the urli has a ceremonial role, holding oil for the brass lamps that are floated in it or receiving offerings of fruit and garlands, and the wide bowl is also used as a base into which a tall traditional oil lamp is set. Because brass is durable and easily polished, old urulis are passed down as household treasures, and the vessel appears in Malayali folk memory as a wedding gift, an heirloom and a standard prop of the naturalistic home garden.
source: South Indian household and wedding practice

name: Banarasi Sari
description: The Banarasi sari is the handwoven silk sari of Varanasi (Banaras) in Uttar Pradesh, famous for its rich brocade, its gold and silver zari, and its intricate pictorial motifs, among them the jangla (vine), bel (creeper), kalga and jal patterns. The weaving tradition grew under the patronage of the Mughal court, which encouraged Persian-inspired floral and arabesque designs in silk and metal thread, and the craft produced the heavy, opulent fabric called kinkhab, woven with real gold thread. A Banarasi sari is woven on a manually operated pit loom, and a single elaborate piece can take weeks or months of work by a karigar, the brocade being built up in fine threads on the wrong side of the cloth. The sari is the classic bridal costume of the region, worn as a symbol of marriage and prosperity, and its silk is still produced in the workshops of the old city, though zari is now often of silver or imitation. In 2009 the Banarasi sari received a Geographical Indication tag, protecting the name for genuine Varanasi work.

name: Butterfly Jigha
description: The butterfly jigha is a jewel-set turban ornament of Mughal court fashion, shaped as a butterfly with wings that tremble on a spring as the wearer moves, pinned to the front of the turban by princes, nobles and high officials. Such ornaments are shown in Mughal miniature painting and in later court portraiture of the Deccan and the regions that became Pakistan, where the jigha, sarpesh and other turban jewels marked rank and the favour of the ruler. Surviving examples worked in gold and enamel with rubies, emeralds and pearls sometimes include a socket for a heron or egret plume that rose above the turban, a feature historically restricted to the royal family and those granted the privilege. The butterfly form with its quivering spring is one of the most recognisable types in museum collections, prized for the delicate chasing and stone-setting of the court jewellers.
source: Museum holdings (e.g. V&A O73036) and Mughal painting

name: Bhutanese Festival Mask
description: The Bhutanese festival mask is a carved and painted wooden face worn by dancers in the cham dances of Bhutanese monasteries, taking the forms of fierce deities, animals, black-hatted dancers and the skeleton guardians of the faith. The tradition of cham is said to have been brought to the Himalayan world by the teacher Padmasambhava, and the dances are performed in the courtyards of the dzongs during the yearly tsechu festivals, when onlookers gather to see the masked dancers turn in slow circles to drum and cymbal. Each mask follows strict iconographic rules, and the identities of the dancers are kept within the monasteries, while the lay people watch and are held to receive blessing and protection from the performance. The festival masks are made by Bhutanese carvers, painted with mineral colours, and are among the most recognisable art forms of the kingdom.

name: Boomerang
description: The boomerang is the curved throwing stick of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, carved from hardwood and used for hunting, fighting, digging and ceremony. Returning boomerangs are shaped with a twist across the wings so that they curve in flight and come back to the thrower, while heavier non-returning forms are hurled flat and low to strike game or an enemy, and the same shapes were used as clapsticks, digging tools and fire-sticks. The weapons are sometimes engraved or painted with the designs of the maker's clan. The returning boomerang is one of the oldest known engineered tools and was taken up worldwide as a sport object, while in Australia the boomerang remains an emblem of Aboriginal skill and appears in Dreaming stories and modern cultural display.
source: Archaeological and ethnographic studies of Aboriginal technology

name: Bullroarer
description: The bullroarer is an oval wooden slat whirled on the end of a cord to produce a low, roaring hum, used by the Aboriginal peoples of Australia in initiation and ceremony. As the slat spins, it cuts the air and the pitch rises and falls with the speed of the whirling, and the sound can carry across a surprising distance. In south-eastern Australia the voice of the bullroarer is sometimes said to be the voice of the ancestor Daramulum, and in many traditions the instrument is kept for the men's law, so that women and children are not shown it. The bullroarer is found in many parts of the world, but in Australia it is bound to the initiation grounds, where its humming warns of the sacred ceremonies taking place and draws the attention of the ancestors to the land.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Aboriginal initiation rites

name: Bilum (Loop String Bag)
description: Loop-woven string bag made and worn by women across Papua New Guinea, worked in a continuous spiral of knotless looping that varies in gauge and pattern from region to region. Carried on the head, over the shoulder or around the neck, it holds garden produce, firewood and bush tucker, and in the Highlands it cradles infants, who travel in a woman's bilum until they can walk. Made originally from bush vines and bark fibre and today often from brightly coloured synthetic yarn, a single bilum can take weeks of work and carries meaning in every stitch. Bilums are given as prestigious gifts at marriage, childbirth, feasts and mourning rites, and their designs and colours can mark the wearer's clan and homeland.
source: Ethnographic records of Highlands material culture

name: Bogrács
description: The bogrács is the black cast-iron cauldron of Hungarian outdoor cooking, a three-legged pot suspended from a chain over an open fire, in which gulyás, pörkölt and fish stew are boiled and stirred with a long wooden spoon. The vessel dates from the world of the herdsmen of the Hungarian Plain, who cooked their one-pot meals over campfires, and the same pot is still the centrepiece of bográcsgulyás gatherings at weekends, feasts and village festivals. Its size and weight vary from small two-litre pots to great cauldrons for hundreds of eaters, and the cast iron is seasoned by use, giving the stew its characteristic smoky savour. Cooking in the bogrács is a slow, sociable ritual - the meat is seared, onion and paprika added, and the pot tended for hours - and for many Hungarians the cauldron over flame is the very image of hospitality and good eating.

name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
description: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are among the most iconic props of Russian folk narrative. Folklorists note that the mortar echoes the work of grain-pounding and the boundary between the farmstead and the wild, fitting the witch who lives at the edge of the forest. She is sometimes said to fly at great speed, using the pestle as her engine and the broom to erase her traces so that pursuers cannot follow. The trio of mortar, pestle and broom has passed into art, film and illustration wherever Baba Yaga appears, and remains instantly recognisable even outside Slavic tradition.

name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
description: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its bright, percussive tone carries well in open-air music-making. The body is usually of spruce or maple, with three strings historically of gut and now of nylon or metal, and the left hand often uses a single downward stroke that produces the crisp, rhythmic drive of dance tunes. Andreyev's balalaika orchestra, founded in 1888, gave the instrument respectability and set off a craze for balalaika ensembles across Europe. It remains the best-known Russian folk instrument abroad, appearing in concert halls, films and comedy routines alike, and its solo repertoire is still taught in Russian music schools.
era: attested from the 17th century; standardised late 19th century
source: Russian folk music tradition; Andreyev's balalaika orchestra (1888)

name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
description: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends from the older kobza and spread across Ukraine from at least the 18th century. In performance the player fingers the melody on the neck while sweeping across the accompaniment strings on the soundboard, producing a resonant, harp-like texture. The blind kobzars who wandered the villages singing historical ballads were famed for long improvisations, and the term 'kobzar' became a byword for the wandering epic singer. The instrument survived the suppression of the kobzar guilds in the Soviet era and is now taught in conservatories, performed in ensembles, and honoured at festivals of Ukrainian music.
material: wood body, gut or metal strings
era: attested from at least the 18th century
source: Ukrainian bandura tradition; studies of the dumy epics

name: Bychakh (Yakut Knife)
description: Traditional knife of the Yakut (Sakha) people, with an asymmetric blade bearing a fuller on one side and a convex edge on the other, a birch-burl handle and a leather sheath. Forged by Yakut blacksmiths from local iron since pre-Russian times, it is used for carving wood, dressing hides and preparing fish and meat, an everyday tool with a remarkably constant design. The blade is set into a short, rounded handle of birch burl, and the whole knife, worn at the belt in a wooden-lined leather sheath, fits the hand so well that it can be used for hours without fatigue. Yakut smithing was famed in Siberia: local marsh iron was smelted and worked into knives, and the blacksmith's trade was held in such honour that it was treated as almost sacred. The bychakh is carried by men for nearly every task of taiga and farm life, and examples found in old burials show the same form as knives made today. It is sometimes said that a good Yakut knife is judged by its balance and by the feel of the birch-burl handle.
material: locally smelted iron, birch burl handle, leather sheath
era: ancient; similar knives found in Yakut burial grounds
source: Wikipedia 'Yakutian knife'; ar.culture.ru 'Yakutian knife'; Russian Museum of Ethnography

name: Buryat Shaman's Drum (Hese)
description: Oval single-headed frame drum of the Buryat shaman (bo), fitted with a cross-shaped handle and a rawhide head often painted with images of animals and the world tree. Struck to summon spirits and to carry the shaman between the worlds, the drum (hese) is the central instrument of Buryat ritual practice; obtaining one marked the shaman's consecration. The frame is bent from a single strip of wood, the head is stretched over it, and the inside carries an iron cross that the shaman grips with the thumb and fingers. The drum is beaten with a padded mallet, and its rhythm varies with the rite: slow strokes for the long journeys to the upper world, quick ones for warding off hostile spirits. A new drum was consecrated at the shaman's initiation, and the first sound it made was sometimes said to reveal which ancestors' spirits would assist him. Ethnographic collections hold drums painted with the sun and moon, the tree of life and the shaman's animal helpers, each image tied to the songs he sang.
material: wooden frame, rawhide head, iron handle
source: Wierucka, 'Shamanism in the Baikal Region' (2013); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat drum'

name: Buryat Shaman's Horse-Staff
description: Ritual staff of the Buryat shaman, carved from birch wood and topped with a horse's head; senior shamans who had passed the fifth consecration carried iron-tipped versions. In Buryat belief the horse-staff served as the shaman's mount to ride through the spirit world, and it remains a recognised emblem of Buryat shamanic practice alongside the drum. The staff is held upright in the ritual tent, its butt struck on the ground to punctuate the songs, and its carved horse-head top is draped with ribbons and small bells. The iron-tipped staff was a privilege of the senior shaman, and a shaman's degree was read in part from the staff he carried and the number of drums he owned. When a shaman died, his staff and drums were sometimes left in the forest at the place of his last ritual. The custom links Buryat practice to a wide Inner Asian pattern, in which the shaman rides a staff or drum as a steed into the spirit realm.
source: Czaplicka, 'Shamanism in Siberia' (1914); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat shaman's staff'
